records.title: Parkes observations for project P1411 semester 2026APRS_28
records.description: Conventional blind pulsar surveys that search for periodic signals in high-time-resolution data are increasingly limited by interstellar scattering at high dispersion measure (DM), orbital modulation in compact binaries, scintillation effects, and intensive computational demands. The Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey provides ultra-deep radio continuum maps enabling complementary image-domain pulsar searches that bypass these limitations. We have discovered seven new pulsars through three targeted strategies: (1) identifying compact sources embedded in supernova remnants (SNRs) and pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), (2) detecting highly variable sources via variance imaging, and (3) selecting highly circularly polarised compact sources. Our sample includes three highly scattered pulsars (PSR J1638-4713 , PSR J1643-4511, and PSR J1631-4722 with DM > 800 pc/cm^3) including two pulsars associated with PWNe. Two millisecond pulsars (PSR J0927-7641 and PSR J1838-5949) are in potential wide binary systems with orbital periods of several tens of days, and two additional normal pulsars (PSR J1153-7106 and PSR 2223-0654). We propose follow-up timing observations of these pulsars with Murriyang's Ultra-Wideband Low (UWL) receiver to obtain phase-connected timing solutions, measure precise positions and spin parameters, and determine orbital characteristics for the binary systems,. These observations will enable studies of pulsar formation mechanisms, binary evolution pathways, PWN-SNR interactions, and validate image-based discovery techniques as powerful complements to traditional blind surveys for detecting elusive pulsars.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1410 semester 2026APRS_11
records.description: Neutron stars are compact remnants formed in core-collapse supernovae of massive stars. A subset of these objects, known as pulsars, emit highly regular pulses of radiation that make them powerful tools for studying fundamental physics, stellar evolution, and the structure of our Galaxy. Despite decades of surveys, the known pulsar population remains incomplete: while about 4,800 pulsars are currently catalogued, population studies predict that roughly 10,000 or more radio-detectable pulsars should be observable with our current instrumentation. A significant fraction of the missing population is expected to consist of slowly rotating pulsars, which are difficult to detect with standard search pipelines. These pulsars often have very narrow pulse duty cycles and long spin periods, making them susceptible to reduced signal-to-noise ratios and contamination by low-frequency ("red") noise in Fourier-based searches. As a result, many such objects may remain hidden in archival survey data. Motivated by this, we reprocessed archival data from the Parkes Multibeam Pulsar Survey targeting narrow-duty-cycle signals and allowing to investigate lower signal to noise ratios for these candidates. This approach led to the identification of 12 highly credible new slow pulsar candidates that were missed in previous analyses. Several of these candidates show strong folded signal-to-noise ratios and physically plausible dispersion measures, indicating they are likely genuine pulsars. The primary goal of this proposal is to obtain targeted follow-up observations to confirm and time these newly identified pulsar candidates. Confirming them will help close the gap between predicted and observed pulsar populations and demonstrate the continued scientific value of archival radio survey data.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1365 semester 2026APRS_13
records.description: Following the successful demonstration of a pilot first-pass (shallow) search of a small fraction of the sky, the second-pass processing has commenced for the SMART pulsar survey, which involves deep searches of 80-minute observations. Over the past year, this second-pass processing has led to the discovery of 16 new pulsars (including two millisecond pulsars), bringing the total number of SMART discoveries to 20 when combined with the first-pass results. These outcomes hint at the exciting promise of this first southern-sky pulsar survey in the frequency band of SKA-Low. All new pulsars require timing observations to determine their spin and astrometric parameters. Another important aspect of timing newly discovered pulsars is to identify specialised targets for further detailed follow-ups. Since the MWA no longer supports routine pulsar observations from 2025, timing follow-ups rely on other telescopes. The Parkes Murriyang telescope, with an identical sky coverage, sensitivity and the wide frequency coverage, offers the best option to time SMART discoveries. We have demonstrated Murriyang's suitability for this through previous semesters and are now extending the project to a sample of 11 pulsars, including six from the last semester. The data will also allow us to study pulse profiles, polarisation, and flux densities from ~100 MHz to 4 GHz. The analysis/results will be included in a publication in preparation that will detail the deep-search pipeline and report on initial pulsar discoveries.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L124 semester 2026APRS_09
records.description: We propose a long-term project to monitor a very active repeater, FRB 20190520B, with Murriyang's UWL system. Our previous observations show that FRB 20190520B is not only among the most active FRBs that can be observed with Murriyang, but also shows extreme rotation measure (RM) and dispersion measure (DM) evolution, along with distinctive behavior at 3GHz frequency. This makes the UWL receiver uniquely suited for detailed studies and long-term monitoring of this repeating FRB. Through this program, we anticipate detecting a large sample of bursts from this FRB. In collaboration with FAST, we aim to investigate the time evolution of various properties of FRB 20190520B, enhance our understanding of polarisation across an extremely wide bandwidth with high sensitivity, and gain deeper insights into the local environment and emission mechanisms of FRBs.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1420 semester 2026APRS_07
records.description: We propose the pilot of a Murriyang CryoPAF Pulsar Survey of the Southern Galactic Plane (CPS-LowLat Pilot). The revolutionary CryoPAF receiver delivers the highest pulsar survey speed in the Southern Hemisphere, exceeding L-band capability of MeerKAT by ~2x, with a sufficiently low data rate to enable archiving and reprocessing essential to maximizing survey yields. Population synthesis predicts ~300 new pulsars in the full CPS-LowLat. Up to ~90 pulsars are predicted from this Pilot in a rich region of the Galactic Plane (-15deg < l < -10deg, |b| < 3deg), including 5-10 millisecond pulsars. 2.5-hr pointings are proposed to provide the requisite transformational pulsar detection rate, while maintaining sensitivity across a wide range of binary orbital periods, including ultra-compact systems. A frequency range of 1.3-1.85 GHz will mitigate dispersion smearing and scattering. Well-developed GPU-based searches for accelerated / binary systems and efficient coherent folding algorithms will be deployed. New discoveries from CPS-LowLat will enable strong-field tests of general relativity, equation-of-state constraints from massive neutron stars, more accurate modeling of the neutron star merger rate, and probes of exotic stellar-evolution pathways and of the ionised interstellar medium. Besides its impressive pulsar yield and the associated scientific possibilities, the proposed pilot will demonstrate the end-to-end performance of the CryoPAF for pulsar surveys prior to commencing the full CPS-LowLat, and validate pulsar population models.

records.description: This is a proposal to search for pulsars in the Globular Cluster NGC6540, with a particular focus on the source 3XMM J180608.9-27455. Its peculiar X-ray variability makes it an intriguing candidate millisecond pulsar. Finding radio pulsations from this source will help unveiling its nature and may reveal the presence of a rare transitional millisecond pulsar. Previous radio observations of this cluster reached relatively shallow flux density and luminosity upper limits, leaving open the possibility to find, with a deeper search such as the one proposed here with the Ultra Wideband Low receiver, more pulsars, possibly also associated with other known point-like X-ray sources in this cluster. In order to achieve this goal, we ask to observe this target for 3 hours twice. The second observation will serve as a confirmation for any candidate we would find in the first and will enhance the chances to find a radio signal also from an eclipsing binary pulsar.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1413 semester 2026APRS_20
records.description: We request 75 hours of Parkes observing time for dedicated radio follow-up observations of PSR J1635-5134, a promising candidate pulsar-subdwarf B (sdB) star binary system. PSR J1635-5134 is a non-recycled 340 ms pulsar in a nearly circular 18-hour orbit with a minimum companion mass of 0.26 solar mass. It lies in a sparsely populated region of binary-pulsars parameter space and may represent a short-lived evolutionary stage immediately following inefficient spin-up, thereby providing a missing link between canonical binaries and the millisecond pulsar-WD population. The system exhibits peculiar, orbital-phase-dependent dispersion-measure (DM) variability, with DM variations exceeding 30 pc/cc, indicating substantial ionised material plausibly associated with an outflow from the companion. Moreover, during prior monitoring with Parkes, the DM variations shifted from being predominantly modest to being persistently large, implying an evolving plasma environment that cannot be characterised with sparse or irregular observations. Determining whether these high-DM variations are intermittent or long-lived, and mapping how the excess material varies with orbital phase and epoch, are essential for constraining the origin and geometry of the plasma and for testing the hypothesis that an sdB wind supplies the required electron column. Through this proposal, we aim to (i) extend the timing baseline to improve astrometric precision to sub-arcsecond accuracy, enabling secure identification of the optical counterpart in a crowded field, and (ii) perform phase-targeted observations during eclipse/DM variation phases to understand the temporal behavior of excess DM.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1379 semester 2026APRS_11
records.description: We propose a simultaneous joint observation campaign using the Parkes radio telescope and the EP satellite to observation three magnetars with known radio emission. Under simultaneous observations, we aim to investigate the correlation between their radio and X-ray emissions, including pulse profiles, flux intensity, polarization evolution, correlated multi-wavelength behavior and timing behavior.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1423 semester 2026APRS_16
records.description: Pulsars are rapidly rotating, highly magnetized neutron stars whose radio emission provides unique probes of extreme gravity, plasma physics, and magnetospheric processes. Millisecond pulsars(MSPs) exhibit exceptional rotational stability, making them fundamental components of Pulsar Timing Arrays used to detect nanohertz gravitational waves, while also enabling precision tests of general relativity, binary evolution, and studies of the interstellar medium(ISM). Normal pulsars(NPs), on the other hand, serve as powerful laboratories for investigating neutron-star interiors, supernova remnants, magnetospheric physics, pulsar winds, and glitch phenomena. Their polarization measurements are crucial, as they constrain emission geometry, magnetic-field configuration, and propagation effects such as Faraday rotation, while enabling robust determination of rotation measures(RM). For MSPs in particular, polarization studies improve timing-template fidelity and help correct frequency-dependent propagation effects that impact high-precision timing experiments. GMRT low-frequency surveys have significantly expanded the known pulsar population, yet many GMRT-discovered pulsars lack broadband polarization measurements, leaving their emission geometry and frequency-dependent profile evolution poorly constrained. We propose 21 hours of observations with the Parkes 64-m telescope using UWL receiver to conduct a spectro-polarimetric study of six GMRT-discovered pulsars: three MSPs(J1207-5050, J1227-4853, J1646-2142) and three NPs(J0514-4407, J0418-4154, J0702-4956) to conduct a spectro-polarimetric study. These targets exhibit unresolved or contradictory polarization behaviour, including profile evolution, eclipse-driven interaction signatures, incomplete detections, or absence of full-Stokes information. The proposed wideband, high-sensitivity observations will provide robust RM measurements, broadband polarization profiles, and frequency-dependent beam mapping, filling key observational gaps and enhancing the scientific value of GMRT-discovered pulsars for magnetospheric studies and pulsar timing science.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P960 semester 2026APRS_09
records.description: We aim to carry out receiver pointing and characterisation tests of Parkes receivers. Typically, these tests are carried out after the receiver package is installed, but time does not always allow for proper characterisation. Receivers for consideration include UWL, MARS and 13MM packages. In addition to cross-referencing C007 for flux calibration via pointing, we aim to conduct gain-elevation and system temperature experiments using the Moon, to ensure users of the Parkes Observatory have the most accurate information available for calibration purposes.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P595 semester 2026APRS_31
records.description: We propose to continue the PULSE@Parkes project in which high school students from Australia and around the World use the Parkes radio telescope in a remote observing model to observe and analyse pulsar data. The data from some PULSE@Parkes observations are used to support the space missions, other observations supplement the P456 Pulsar Timing Array project and the remainder were chosen in order to make a detailed analysis of pulsar timing irregularities and intermittency.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1416 semester 2026APRS_05
records.description: Radio pulsars in orbit around high-mass stellar companions offer a rich source of extreme physics for both observational astronomers and theorists alike. Despite being discovered 25 years ago, PSR J1638-4725 remains a veritable mystery compared to similar pulsar binary systems. Long-term monitoring has revealed extended `eclipses' where the pulsar is undetectable for months around periastron at GHz frequencies, along with intense variations in the observed pulsar dispersion measure, scatter broadening and flux density throughout the entire orbit. Preliminary spectroscopic characterisation of the companion star suggests it may be an O/B star, albiet one without a circumstellar disc of ejected material. This raises the unique opportunity to answer test the structure and origin of the near-wind regime of high-mass stars. In this proposal we will conduct an ambitious monitoring campaign of PSR J1638-4725 with both the ultra-wideband low and MARS recievers on Murriyang. We will track changes in the pulsar dispersion and scattering as it swings around the companion star, providing unique insights into the density and temperature distribution of the stellar wind from the companion star before and after the pulsar swings through periastron. These observations will also play a pivotal role in a broader multi-wavelength campaign to fully capture the upcoming 2026 periastron passage.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1375 semester 2026APRS_09
records.description: Rotating radio transients (RRATs) are Galactic neutron stars that emit sporadic radio pulses, and the question of whether apparently one-off sources truly repeat remains unresolved. With the discovery of numerous fast radio bursts (FRBs), the paradigm of 'one detection defines an astrophysical source' has shifted. However, the distinction between truly non-repeating Galactic transients and insufficiently observed repeating sources remains critical. Recent high-sensitivity follow-up observations with FAST have revealed that multiple apparent one-off RRATs originally detected by Parkes are in fact repeating sources, with fainter pulses hundreds of times weaker than their initial bright detections. This discovery raises a fundamental question: are many one-off RRATs simply the result of insufficient observational sensitivity, or do they represent intrinsically catastrophic transient events. We propose deep follow-up monitoring of four apparent one-off RRATs using the Parkes Ultra-Wideband receiver system, which offers 1.7-3.4 times higher sensitivity than the Multibeam discovery data. These observations will constrain the pulse repetition rates and energy distributions of these sources, examine the extreme variability seen in some RRATs and pulsars that exhibit pulses differing by >500 times in brightness, and test whether hidden repeating emission explains the apparent one-off nature of these sources.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1421 semester 2026APRS_01
records.description: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, ultra-bright transients, most likely associated with neutron stars. Although their luminosity makes them powerful probes of cosmological environments, their extragalactic distances and sporadic occurrence hinder direct investigation of their emission physics. The Crab pulsar has been considered a potential Galactic analogue to FRBs through its giant pulses (GPs). At nanosecond resolution, Crab GPs resolve into narrowband, nearly 100% polarised nanoshots with randomly distributed polarisation angles (PAs), motivating models in which burst envelopes arise from the superposition of many independently polarised shots. However, this behaviour contrasts with most FRBs, which frequently exhibit coherent PA evolution across microsecond-millisecond timescales. Consequently, Crab GPs have generally been regarded as poor FRB analogues. Recent high-time-resolution observations from the CRAFT survey revealed FRBs with rapid, highly structured PA variability that is naturally interpreted as the superposition of partially correlated polarised shots rather than smooth PA swings. Also, a rare and largely unexplored sub-class of Crab single pulses has been identified that exhibits coherent or partially ordered PA evolution on nanosecond-microsecond timescales, implying correlated shot properties or organised plasma and magnetic-field structure within the emission region. We aim to systematically identify and characterise these Crab pulses and assess their relevance as FRB analogues. Using the Fast, Intense Radio Emission Simulator (FIRES), we model these events within a polarised shot noise framework and directly compare their inferred shot properties to the high-time-resolution CRAFT FRB sample.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1409 semester 2026APRS_07
records.description: To investigate the physical origin and local environment of the repeating fast radio burst FRB 20230607A, which exhibits an exceptionally high rotation measure, we propose to observe this repeater with 24-hour observations using the Ultra-Wideband Low-frequency (UWL) receiver of the Parkes radio telescope (Murriyang). This proposal aims to monitor the secular evolution of the Faraday Rotation Measure, studying the cause of its low linear polarization, and resolve the specro-polarimetric structure of repeat bursts. The possible findings are critical to unveiling the extreme magnetized environment of the source, understanding emission mechanisms and propagation effects, and thereby shedding light on the physics origin(s) of repeating fast radio bursts.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1411 semester 2026APRS_31
records.description: Conventional blind pulsar surveys that search for periodic signals in high-time-resolution data are increasingly limited by interstellar scattering at high dispersion measure (DM), orbital modulation in compact binaries, scintillation effects, and intensive computational demands. The Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey provides ultra-deep radio continuum maps enabling complementary image-domain pulsar searches that bypass these limitations. We have discovered seven new pulsars through three targeted strategies: (1) identifying compact sources embedded in supernova remnants (SNRs) and pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), (2) detecting highly variable sources via variance imaging, and (3) selecting highly circularly polarised compact sources. Our sample includes three highly scattered pulsars (PSR J1638-4713 , PSR J1643-4511, and PSR J1631-4722 with DM > 800 pc/cm^3) including two pulsars associated with PWNe. Two millisecond pulsars (PSR J0927-7641 and PSR J1838-5949) are in potential wide binary systems with orbital periods of several tens of days, and two additional normal pulsars (PSR J1153-7106 and PSR 2223-0654). We propose follow-up timing observations of these pulsars with Murriyang's Ultra-Wideband Low (UWL) receiver to obtain phase-connected timing solutions, measure precise positions and spin parameters, and determine orbital characteristics for the binary systems,. These observations will enable studies of pulsar formation mechanisms, binary evolution pathways, PWN-SNR interactions, and validate image-based discovery techniques as powerful complements to traditional blind surveys for detecting elusive pulsars.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1365 semester 2026APRS_15
records.description: Following the successful demonstration of a pilot first-pass (shallow) search of a small fraction of the sky, the second-pass processing has commenced for the SMART pulsar survey, which involves deep searches of 80-minute observations. Over the past year, this second-pass processing has led to the discovery of 16 new pulsars (including two millisecond pulsars), bringing the total number of SMART discoveries to 20 when combined with the first-pass results. These outcomes hint at the exciting promise of this first southern-sky pulsar survey in the frequency band of SKA-Low. All new pulsars require timing observations to determine their spin and astrometric parameters. Another important aspect of timing newly discovered pulsars is to identify specialised targets for further detailed follow-ups. Since the MWA no longer supports routine pulsar observations from 2025, timing follow-ups rely on other telescopes. The Parkes Murriyang telescope, with an identical sky coverage, sensitivity and the wide frequency coverage, offers the best option to time SMART discoveries. We have demonstrated Murriyang's suitability for this through previous semesters and are now extending the project to a sample of 11 pulsars, including six from the last semester. The data will also allow us to study pulse profiles, polarisation, and flux densities from ~100 MHz to 4 GHz. The analysis/results will be included in a publication in preparation that will detail the deep-search pipeline and report on initial pulsar discoveries.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1402 semester 2026APRS_22
records.description: We propose a dedicated Parkes/Murriyang timing campaign of the newly confirmed narrow-duty cycle (~6 %) millisecond pulsar (MSP) PSR J2147-3604. This source was identified in a reprocessing of the Green Bank North Celestial Cap (GBNCC) survey as a high-confidence candidate with a spin period of 3.2 ms, and a dispersion measure, DM of 17 pc/cc. The pulsar was subsequently confirmed by the Fermi--TRAPUM collaboration via MeerKAT beamforming localisation and Parkes follow-up. Parkes/UWL observations allocated using green time detected this pulsar between 700--1500~MHz, and confirmed that it's in a binary system. Due to its low DM, we also detected strong interstellar scintillation. We request 35~hr of Murriyang time using the UWL receiver and APOLLO backend to obtain a phase-coherent timing solution and to characterise its spin, orbital, and propagation properties. Since the pulsar is also associated with a FERMI source, a precise radio ephemeris will also enable sensitive searches for gamma-ray pulsations in Fermi-LAT data and assess PSR J2147-3604's suitability for pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) and future gamma-ray timing applications.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1418 semester 2026APRS_06
records.description: Pulsars exhibit diverse radio-emission phenomena that remain poorly understoon. Among the most extreme are giant pulses (GPs): short-duration radio bursts whose energies exceed the average pulse by at least 10 times. Only 16 pulsars are known to emit GPs, including just five millisecond pulsars. This rises the question of whether this reflects intrinsic population differences or observational bias. We propose high time-resolution observations with Murriyang Ultra Wide-bandwidth Low-frequency (UWL) receiver to search for and characterise GPs from two prominent millisecond pulsar candidates, PSR J0030+0451 and PSR J1902-5105. Both share key properties with established GP emitters including large magnetic fields at the light-cylinder and high energy emission in X and gamma ray. These observations will provide essential clues to understanding how GPs are generated and what is their relation to average radio and high energy emissions in terms of their production mechanisms and locations within the pulsars magnetosphere.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1375 semester 2026APRS_10
records.description: Rotating radio transients (RRATs) are Galactic neutron stars that emit sporadic radio pulses, and the question of whether apparently one-off sources truly repeat remains unresolved. records.title: Parkes observations for project P1398 semester 2026APRS_13
records.description: Low-frequency (< ~1 GHz) Galactic-plane pulsar surveys are strongly limited by sky background noise, interstellar scattering, and dispersion smearing, leading to an incomplete census of the pulsar population. High-frequency (> 2 GHz) observations mitigate these effects and have recently enabled the discovery of pulsars that remain undetectable at low-frequency. We analyzed archival data from the 2008 Parkes 6.5-GHz pulsar survey using modern search techniques. This reprocessing has revealed four previously unknown millisecond pulsar candidates with spin periods of 3-11 ms and dispersion measures of 20-170 pc/cc. Two candidates exhibit significant line-of-sight acceleration, indicating likely membership in compact binary systems. We request a total of 8.4 hours of follow-up observations with the Parkes (Murriyang) Ultra-Wideband Low (UWL) receiver to confirm these candidates and characterize their emission across 704-4032 MHz. Confirming these sources would expand the population of high-frequency selected pulsars and demonstrate the continued importance of high-frequency searches for uncovering exotic systems obscured in conventional low-frequency surveys.

records.title: River Murray Water Quality Monitoring Program
records.description: Phytoplankton and physico-chemical monitoring along the River Murray were established in 1978 under the River Murray Water Quality Monitoring Program (RMWQMP). The phytoplankton component began with sites spread across NSW, Victoria, and SA from the NSW upper Murray to the SA Lower Lakes. With the number of sites reconciled in 1980, phytoplankton monitoring has continued at 12 sites, with 10 sites along the River Murray and 2 sites near the confluence of the main tributaries, being the Darling and Murrumbidgee rivers. Biological parameters monitored comprise phytoplankton, phycocyanin and chlorophyll-a. For further details refer to accompanying PDF the [phytoplankton metadata statement](https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/river-murray-water-quality-monitoring-program/resource/0e0a5050-8b2f-4ce3-ab16-8b749c0a38bf). The physico-chemical component began with 32 sites along the Murray River and various tributaries, increasing to 35 sites in 1980 then reducing to 28 sites (along with some frequency changes) in 2012. Physico-chemical parameters monitored vary but include temperate, EC, pH, turbidity, colour, TKN, NOx, Total P, FRP, silica, DOC, bicarbonate, sulfate, and metals. The range of parameters and frequency of monitoring undertaken at a site is determined by the site class as described in Physico-chemical meta data statement. For further details refer to accompanying PDF the [physico-chemical metadata statement](https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/river-murray-water-quality-monitoring-program/resource/15d21ea2-9dc2-4136-8600-808608151886).

records.title: Estimated spatial distributions for Australia's threatened species: May 2025
records.description: This data set contains spatial layers of the estimated extant and historical distributions for species listed as Critically Endangered, Endangered, or Vulnerable as of 28 May 2025 and that occurred within the contiguous Australian exclusive economic zone. This includes 1,785 species with terrestrial distributions, 122 species with aquatic distributions, and 95 species with marine distributions, with 1,962 species in total (noting that some species can occur in multiple realms). For each species, their extant and historical distributions were estimated using a simple logical algorithm based on Species of National Environmental Significance Distribution grids (DCCEEW 2025a), occurrence records (ALA 2025), and spatial environmental layers, described in full in Giljohann et al. (2025) and in the Lineage text associated with this data publication.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L125 semester 2026APRS_25
records.description: The atomic interstellar medium shows tiny-scale optical depth fluctuations on the scale of 0.1~10,000 AU, whose origin and nature are poorly understood. The existence of this Tiny-Scale Atomic Structure (TSAS) has significant implications, potentially calling into question our fundamental understanding of heating, cooling and dynamical processes in the interstellar medium. Yet observations remain sparse. This long-term project plans to search for temporal variations in HI absorption spectra seen against background pulsars to characterise TSAS in the Milky Way interstellar medium (ISM). These observations constitute the largest number of sightlines and densest temporal sampling ever performed in a single experiment, and will test predictions that TSAS is the tail end of a turbulent cascade, constrain its minimum size scale (down to resolutions of ~0.05 AU) and potentially provide the first direct measurements of pressures in "large" TSAS features of > 1000 AU. We make use of the phase-resolved spectral line mode that we have recently implemented on Parkes, which has cut data rates and processing times by factors of ~1000 compared to past studies. This is an expansion of our pilot P1321 to a long term study.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1416 semester 2026APRS_06
records.description: Radio pulsars in orbit around high-mass stellar companions offer a rich source of extreme physics for both observational astronomers and theorists alike. Despite being discovered 25 years ago, PSR J1638-4725 remains a veritable mystery compared to similar pulsar binary systems. Long-term monitoring has revealed extended `eclipses' where the pulsar is undetectable for months around periastron at GHz frequencies, along with intense variations in the observed pulsar dispersion measure, scatter broadening and flux density throughout the entire orbit. Preliminary spectroscopic characterisation of the companion star suggests it may be an O/B star, albiet one without a circumstellar disc of ejected material. This raises the unique opportunity to answer test the structure and origin of the near-wind regime of high-mass stars. In this proposal we will conduct an ambitious monitoring campaign of PSR J1638-4725 with both the ultra-wideband low and MARS recievers on Murriyang. We will track changes in the pulsar dispersion and scattering as it swings around the companion star, providing unique insights into the density and temperature distribution of the stellar wind from the companion star before and after the pulsar swings through periastron. These observations will also play a pivotal role in a broader multi-wavelength campaign to fully capture the upcoming 2026 periastron passage.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1390 semester 2026APRS_04
records.description: We propose 18.9 hours of Parkes Ultra-Wideband (UWL) observations to investigate PSR J1606-0854, a remarkable nearby Galactic pulsar discovered via the ASKAP CRACO backend. This source exhibits unprecedented emission properties that challenge conventional classification boundaries: it produces ultra-bright bursts (up to 900 Jy ms) with broad durations (~ 20 ms), extremely faint RRAT-like emission (0.02-0.5 Jy ms), but notably lacks intermediate-fluence pulses (1-10 Jy ms). The fluence distribution spans five orders of magnitude, with a surface magnetic field strength of B_surf ~ 1.3e14 G comparable to magnetars, and is the highest among known RRATs. High-sensitivity FAST observations conducted since July 2025 have detected over 100 pulses. With Parkes complementary sensitivity and wideband spectral coverage (0.7-4 GHz), we will search for the missing intermediate-fluence pulses and characterize the source's broadband spectrum. This study provides a unique laboratory for understanding neutron-star emission mechanisms across an unprecedented dynamic range, probing the faint end of the neutron-star emission continuum, and investigating the evolutionary connections between classical pulsars, rotating radio transients, and magnetars.

records.title: Geomorphic change detection between 2018 and 2024-2025 for the North Bowen region of the Burdekin River Basin Queensland Australia
records.description: This dataset shows geomorphic change (erosion and deposition) in the Bowen-Broken catchment of the Burdekin River Basin Queensland, Australia. The change is determined by the difference in elevation in the overlapping areas of two co-registered airborne laser scanning (ALS) point cloud datasets, collected in 2018 and 2024-2025. The change is measured in metres for each 0.5 m x 0.5 m grid cell across the study area. Negative values indicate erosion and positive values indicate deposition.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1398 semester 2026APRS_14
records.description: Low-frequency (< ~1 GHz) Galactic-plane pulsar surveys are strongly limited by sky background noise, interstellar scattering, and dispersion smearing, leading to an incomplete census of the pulsar population. High-frequency (> 2 GHz) observations mitigate these effects and have recently enabled the discovery of pulsars that remain undetectable at low-frequency. We analyzed archival data from the 2008 Parkes 6.5-GHz pulsar survey using modern search techniques. This reprocessing has revealed four previously unknown millisecond pulsar candidates with spin periods of 3-11 ms and dispersion measures of 20-170 pc/cc. Two candidates exhibit significant line-of-sight acceleration, indicating likely membership in compact binary systems. We request a total of 8.4 hours of follow-up observations with the Parkes (Murriyang) Ultra-Wideband Low (UWL) receiver to confirm these candidates and characterize their emission across 704-4032 MHz. Confirming these sources would expand the population of high-frequency selected pulsars and demonstrate the continued importance of high-frequency searches for uncovering exotic systems obscured in conventional low-frequency surveys.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P960 semester 2026APRS_10

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1411 semester 2026APRS_32
records.description: Conventional blind pulsar surveys that search for periodic signals in high-time-resolution data are increasingly limited by interstellar scattering at high dispersion measure (DM), orbital modulation in compact binaries, scintillation effects, and intensive computational demands. The Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey provides ultra-deep radio continuum maps enabling complementary image-domain pulsar searches that bypass these limitations. We have discovered seven new pulsars through three targeted strategies: (1) identifying compact sources embedded in supernova remnants (SNRs) and pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), (2) detecting highly variable sources via variance imaging, and (3) selecting highly circularly polarised compact sources. Our sample includes three highly scattered pulsars (PSR J1638-4713 , PSR J1643-4511, and PSR J1631-4722 with DM > 800 pc/cm^3) including two pulsars associated with PWNe. Two millisecond pulsars (PSR J0927-7641 and PSR J1838-5949) are in potential wide binary systems with orbital periods of several tens of days, and two additional normal pulsars (PSR J1153-7106 and PSR 2223-0654). We propose follow-up timing observations of these pulsars with Murriyang's Ultra-Wideband Low (UWL) receiver to obtain phase-connected timing solutions, measure precise positions and spin parameters, and determine orbital characteristics for the binary systems,. These observations will enable studies of pulsar formation mechanisms, binary evolution pathways, PWN-SNR interactions, and validate image-based discovery techniques as powerful complements to traditional blind surveys for detecting elusive pulsars.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1410 semester 2026APRS_12
records.description: Neutron stars are compact remnants formed in core-collapse supernovae of massive stars. A subset of these objects, known as pulsars, emit highly regular pulses of radiation that make them powerful tools for studying fundamental physics, stellar evolution, and the structure of our Galaxy. Despite decades of surveys, the known pulsar population remains incomplete: while about 4,800 pulsars are currently catalogued, population studies predict that roughly 10,000 or more radio-detectable pulsars should be observable with our current instrumentation. A significant fraction of the missing population is expected to consist of slowly rotating pulsars, which are difficult to detect with standard search pipelines. These pulsars often have very narrow pulse duty cycles and long spin periods, making them susceptible to reduced signal-to-noise ratios and contamination by low-frequency ("red") noise in Fourier-based searches. As a result, many such objects may remain hidden in archival survey data. Motivated by this, we reprocessed archival data from the Parkes Multibeam Pulsar Survey targeting narrow-duty-cycle signals and allowing to investigate lower signal to noise ratios for these candidates. This approach led to the identification of 12 highly credible new slow pulsar candidates that were missed in previous analyses. Several of these candidates show strong folded signal-to-noise ratios and physically plausible dispersion measures, indicating they are likely genuine pulsars. The primary goal of this proposal is to obtain targeted follow-up observations to confirm and time these newly identified pulsar candidates. Confirming them will help close the gap between predicted and observed pulsar populations and demonstrate the continued scientific value of archival radio survey data.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L126 semester 2026APRS_16
records.description: We propose a modest program to continue monitoring 4 of the 6 known radio magnetars in order to achieve three primary science goals. The first is to characterise magnetar outbursts over long timescales, for which tracking their rotational, flux density, and polarisation properties provide a clear view of the impulse response of their magnetic fields. Second, understanding the links between magnetars the mysterious fast radio burst phenomenon through the discovery of rare emission and propagation effects, shared spectro-temporal phenomenology, and connections to high-energy (X-ray/gamma-ray) phenomena. Lastly, our continued monitoring has enormous benefit to the wider magnetar community, providing rapid alerts to changes in activity, adding context to unusual behaviour detected by high-energy observations, and a host of supplementary science through the teams extensive collaborative networks. The project and its precursors have been running since 2007 and have contributed to 22 publications since then. This is the first submission since the project was converted to long-term status.

records.title: RV Investigator Voyage IN2023_V04 (INIV) Data Products
records.description: This record describes the quality-controlled data products from the Marine National Facility (MNF) RV Investigator voyage IN2023_V04, titled "International nutrient inter-comparison study in the Southern Ocean: quantifying and identifying the causes of differences in dissolved inorganic nutrient datasets between global seagoing laboratories - Phase 2" (INIV). The voyage took place between June 5, 2023 and June 18, 2023 (AEST), departing from Hobart and returning to Hobart. For further information please refer to the voyage documentation links. The INIV data products have been created by the following teams: CSIRO Data Acquisition and Processing: Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP; 75, 150 KHz ), CTD, Lowered ADCP (LADCP), Underway (UWY), Infrared Sea Surface Temperature Autonomous Radiometer (ISAR) CSIRO Hydrochemistry: Hydrochemistry (HYD) CSIRO Geophysical Systems and Mapping: Fisheries Echosounder (EK80), Multibeam Echosounders (EM710, EM122), Sub-bottom Profiler (SBP120) CSIRO Multiphase Atmospheric Chemistry: Scanning Mobility Particle Sizers (SMPS) CSIRO Ocean Carbon Observations: pCO2 CSIRO Ocean Dynamics: Expendable Bathythermographs (XBTs) ANSTO Atmospheric Research: Radon sensor Voyage Science Participant Data: CRM nutrients, CTD nutrients The datasets are curated by the CSIRO National Collections and Marine Infrastructure (NCMI) Information and Data Centre (IDC) in Hobart, with a permanent public archive at the CSIRO Data Access Portal (https://data.csiro.au/). All processed data from this voyage are also made publicly available through the MNF Data Trawler (in the related links). All voyage documentation is available electronically to MNF support via the local network. Applications to access voyage documentation by non-CSIRO participants can be made via data-requests-hf@csiro.au.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1413 semester 2026APRS_21
records.description: We request 75 hours of Parkes observing time for dedicated radio follow-up observations of PSR J1635-5134, a promising candidate pulsar-subdwarf B (sdB) star binary system. PSR J1635-5134 is a non-recycled 340 ms pulsar in a nearly circular 18-hour orbit with a minimum companion mass of 0.26 solar mass. It lies in a sparsely populated region of binary-pulsars parameter space and may represent a short-lived evolutionary stage immediately following inefficient spin-up, thereby providing a missing link between canonical binaries and the millisecond pulsar-WD population. The system exhibits peculiar, orbital-phase-dependent dispersion-measure (DM) variability, with DM variations exceeding 30 pc/cc, indicating substantial ionised material plausibly associated with an outflow from the companion. Moreover, during prior monitoring with Parkes, the DM variations shifted from being predominantly modest to being persistently large, implying an evolving plasma environment that cannot be characterised with sparse or irregular observations. Determining whether these high-DM variations are intermittent or long-lived, and mapping how the excess material varies with orbital phase and epoch, are essential for constraining the origin and geometry of the plasma and for testing the hypothesis that an sdB wind supplies the required electron column. Through this proposal, we aim to (i) extend the timing baseline to improve astrometric precision to sub-arcsecond accuracy, enabling secure identification of the optical counterpart in a crowded field, and (ii) perform phase-targeted observations during eclipse/DM variation phases to understand the temporal behavior of excess DM.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1406 semester 2026APRS_06
records.description: NGC 362 is a post-core-collapse southern globular cluster (GC) where 12 pulsars have recently been discovered. The pulsar population is very diverse, containing extremely fast-spinning, mildly recycled and slow pulsars, the vast majority of which (11 out of 12) are part of binary systems with very different orbital periods and eccentricities. However, a full orbital characterization was possible only for three of these binaries. This is because the pulsars in NGC 362 are heavily affected by scintillation, and therefore are very elusive. Here, we propose to carry out a series of deep observations of NGC 362, taking advantage of the ultra-wide bandwidth of the UWL receiver, with the aim of determining the orbital parameters of the 8 binary pulsars that still lack characterization. This is of utmost importance, as it is the prerequisite for the derivation of their timing solutions. The latter would in turn allow a wealth of potential studies, such as probing the presence of a mass excess at the center of NGC 362, looking for optical and X-ray counterparts, studying the magnetic field at arcsecond scales, and more. These kinds of studies are only possible in clusters that host many pulsars. With its 12 pulsars, NGC 362 harbors a huge scientific potential, which we aim to unlock by characterizing its binaries. Moreover, we may discover additional pulsars thanks to fortuitous scintillation events.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1402 semester 2026APRS_23
records.description: We propose a dedicated Parkes/Murriyang timing campaign of the newly confirmed narrow-duty cycle (~6 %) millisecond pulsar (MSP) PSR J2147-3604. This source was identified in a reprocessing of the Green Bank North Celestial Cap (GBNCC) survey as a high-confidence candidate with a spin period of 3.2 ms, and a dispersion measure, DM of 17 pc/cc. The pulsar was subsequently confirmed by the Fermi--TRAPUM collaboration via MeerKAT beamforming localisation and Parkes follow-up. Parkes/UWL observations allocated using green time detected this pulsar between 700--1500~MHz, and confirmed that it's in a binary system. Due to its low DM, we also detected strong interstellar scintillation. We request 35~hr of Murriyang time using the UWL receiver and APOLLO backend to obtain a phase-coherent timing solution and to characterise its spin, orbital, and propagation properties. Since the pulsar is also associated with a FERMI source, a precise radio ephemeris will also enable sensitive searches for gamma-ray pulsations in Fermi-LAT data and assess PSR J2147-3604's suitability for pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) and future gamma-ray timing applications.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L101 semester 2026APRS_07
records.description: The Parkes Pulsar Timing Array (PPTA) project has three primary goals: (a) detection of gravitational waves from astronomical sources, (b) establishment of a pulsar timescale, and (c) improvement of our understanding of Solar-system dynamics. We are now in an exciting regime where a signal detected in our (and other data sets) has the form expected for a gravitational wave background. We, along with the international community, are now working hard to either confirm or deny this result, and to determine the astrophysical origin of this signal. With this proposal, we aim to maintain our pre-eminent position in the field. This is a continuing proposal for which observations of millisecond pulsars (MSPs) will continue to improve bounds on ultra-low-frequency gravitational waves until they are detected with confidence. Continued Parkes observations will remain valuable at least until the first stage of the SKA is able to improve on our sensitivity and observing cadence. Even after the gravitational wave background is detected, continued observations will resolve the background origin and individual sources will be identified; advancing the nascent field of gravitational wave astronomy.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L133 semester 2026APRS_05
records.description: This project is to continue timing and profile studies of the first double-pulsar system, a unique laboratory for gravitational physics. Important results published in our 53-page Phys. Rev. X paper (2021) include the first measurements of higher-order light-propagation effects and of the relativistic deformation of the orbit and highlight the importance of a long term observational campaign, including VLBI observations, for this remarkable system. The main aims of this proposal are to provide the strongest tests to date for general relativity and to measure for the first time the moment-of-inertia of a neutron star. Additionally, we will determine the system geometry, map the pulsar beams via geodetic precession, and search for the reappearance of Pulsar B. We exploit the high sensitivity and broad bandwidth of the UWL receiver. We are collaborating with the MeerKAT Double Pulsar Timing team to optimise combination of MeerKAT and UWL data.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1419 semester 2026APRS_07
records.description: We propose a deep 100-hour Parkes radio pulsar survey of the Galactic plane region l = 240 ~ 260 deg, |b| < 2 deg, -a 80-square-degree zone currently unobserved by any major deep pulsar survey such as the Parkes Multibeam Pulsar Survey (PMPS) and The MPIfR-MeerKAT Galactic Plane Survey (MMGPS). This sightline probes the near side of the Perseus Arm (4~6 kpc), yet contains only 14 known pulsars, likely incomplete due to the shallow integrations and FFT-limited pipelines of prior work. Using the CryoPAF receiver (1100 ~ 1700 MHz, 600 MHz bandwidth) with 3000-second pointings and a Fast Folding Algorithm (FFA)-enhanced search, we will detect long-period (P=1~10s) and high-DM (< 350 pc cm ^-3) pulsars missed previously. We expect to discover 20 ~ 40 new pulsars, enabling precise mapping of the local electron density and testing Galactic ISM models. Critically, our field contains the unassociated Fermi sources , offering a prime opportunity for multiwavelength identification. The survey will also probe transient phenomena via single-pulse searches. This project addresses a well-defined observational gap with high discovery potential for both Galactic structure and high-energy astrophysics.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1375 semester 2026APRS_12
records.description: Rotating radio transients (RRATs) are Galactic neutron stars that emit sporadic radio pulses, and the question of whether apparently one-off sources truly repeat remains unresolved. With the discovery of numerous fast radio bursts (FRBs), the paradigm of 'one detection defines an astrophysical source' has shifted. However, the distinction between truly non-repeating Galactic transients and insufficiently observed repeating sources remains critical. Recent high-sensitivity follow-up observations with FAST have revealed that multiple apparent one-off RRATs originally detected by Parkes are in fact repeating sources, with fainter pulses hundreds of times weaker than their initial bright detections. This discovery raises a fundamental question: are many one-off RRATs simply the result of insufficient observational sensitivity, or do they represent intrinsically catastrophic transient events. We propose deep follow-up monitoring of four apparent one-off RRATs using the Parkes Ultra-Wideband receiver system, which offers 1.7-3.4 times higher sensitivity than the Multibeam discovery data. These observations will constrain the pulse repetition rates and energy distributions of these sources, examine the extreme variability seen in some RRATs and pulsars that exhibit pulses differing by >500 times in brightness, and test whether hidden repeating emission explains the apparent one-off nature of these sources.

records.title: An IMU Dataset for Human Activity Recognition to Support Independent Living in Smart Homes (IMU-HAR-IL)
records.description: HAR-IMU-IL includes recordings of 50 participants performing 17 clinically relevant activities of daily living, spanning four functional domains essential for independent living: mobility, hygiene, nutrition and hydration, and medication management. The dataset was collected using a dense deployment of 30 inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, comprising both wearable and object-mounted devices integrated within a real-world residential setting. Ethics approval to complete this study was obtained from CSIRO's Health and Medical Human Research Ethics Committee, before conducting this study (Approval number: 2024_018_LR). All participants provided informed written consent before participating in the study.

records.title: National biodiversity data for ecosystem accounting in Australia: 1990-2024
records.description: This collection comprises biodiversity data for Australia for use in national ecosystem accounts. The data provided are spatial data and summary tables of predicted status of different biodiversity features across Australia over time. Data are provided separately for two types of biodiversity features: (1) nationally listed threatened species; (2) all native species in broad taxonomic groups (vascular plants, birds, reptiles, fungi). The status of all biodiversity features has been estimated annually, for each year from 1990 to 2024. The data are generated using a habitat-based biodiversity assessment approach, where expected spatial patterns of biodiversity in reference condition are combined with a time series of spatial patterns of in ecosystem condition derived from the Habitat Condition Assessment System (HCAS) version 3.3 (90 m resolution) data collection - ecosystem site condition (see related links). For all biodiversity features, annual patterns of expected (or potential) status were derived by combining remotely sensed data with information on inferred reference patterns in biodiversity (pre-European), incorporating field observation data. These data align with other data prepared for Australia under the National Ecosystem Accounting Project, including for ecosystem extent, ecosystem condition and ecosystem services. The biodiversity data comprise spatial raster layers and summary tables of predicted status of different biodiversity features across Australia over time. Also provided are supplementary data tables, maps and charts.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L134 semester 2026APRS_08
records.description: Omega Cen is the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way. It contains at least 18 known MSPs, and there are solid hints for the presence of an even larger pulsar population. We propose a regular monthly follow-up to refine the timing solutions of the five Parkes discoveries from 2020, and to find timing solutions for the 13 MeerKAT discoveries from 2023, in combination with six MeerKAT observations between 2021 and 2023, and future MeerKAT observations. These timing solutions should enable the detection of derivatives of the spin periods of these pulsars, allowing us to probe the dynamics of Omega Cen and the presence of a possible IMBH at its centre. Timing solutions will also enable the search for X-ray and gamma-ray pulsations in the multiple sources detected in this cluster. This study will allow us to better understand the populations of this globular cluster and its formation history. We request observations until 2030, when we expect to have measurements of the second period derivative of the five brighter discoveries, and first period derivative measurements for the later discoveries. These observations will also contribute to the study of eclipsing binaries, and may include future discoveries from pending searches in MeerKAT data.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1183 semester 2026APRS_11
records.description: After nearly four years of monitoring with both the Parkes and FAST telescopes, FRB 20220529 has been established as an extremely active repeater. It exhibits one of the longest known activity durations and shows evidence for a potential periodicity. Owing to the frequent observations carried out with Parkes and FAST, two abrupt rotation-measure (RM) flares have been detected in this source. These constitute the first RM flares ever observed in a fast radio burst (FRB), indicating that a dense, magnetised plasma clump passed across the line of sight. The second RM flare in particular makes a binary-origin scenario for FRB 20220529 especially compelling. If confirmed, the periodicity and RM flares would mutually reinforce one another, serving as a smoking gun for a binary origin. Previous analyses have shown that observations from both Parkes and FAST are essential. FAST's exceptional sensitivity enables the detection of many bursts, whereas the Parkes UWL receiver provides a stable burst-detection rate even during low-activity phases. To further investigate FRB 20220529, we have scheduled regular FAST observations every fortnight. We therefore propose to continue monitoring FRB 20220529 with the Parkes UWL receiver as well. The FAST and Parkes sessions are expected to be separated by a few days, ideally about one week. A cadence of approximately one week offers an excellent opportunity to capture detailed structure during the onset of RM decreases, as demonstrated by previous monitoring.

records.title: HRT-SA Dataset
records.description: This repository contains a multimodal dataset collected from 30 participants with varying levels of expertise to support the evaluation of methods for assessing human situational awareness (SA) gaps—specifically Perceptual Situational Awareness Latencies (PSALs) and Comprehension Situational Awareness Latencies (CSALs)—during a simulated search-and-rescue human–robot teaming (HRT) mission. The dataset includes: · Eye-tracking data (raw data, preprocessed data, extracted eye-tracking features) · Electrodermal activity (EDA) · Photoplethysmogram (PPG) · Skin temperature · Wrist movement data · Operator interaction data · Robot telemetry and state data · De-identified responses to subjective questionnaires In addition, the dataset provides ground-truth labels for PSALs and CSALs at predefined mission events requiring different forms of operator assistance, including: · Waypoint navigation · Robot teleoperation · Verification of robot-detected objects This dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) license. Use of the dataset must also comply with the applicable institutional ethics requirements. Refer to README_Dataset_Wiki.pdf for details covering: · Ethics Approval · Experimental Setup · Participant Details · Study Procedure · Subjective Data · Sensors and Objective Data · Ground Truth Labels

records.title: A Standard Metadata Template for Representing Sample and Sub-sample Relationships
records.description: This collection contains a metadata template used to define the relationship between a physical sample and its associated sub-samples. The template has been used in the CMR-Specify system to import sub-sample relationships. All individual samples must be catalogued in the system before the relationship template is uploaded. The project short name, project identifier, and sample number provided in the template must exactly match the corresponding curated sample records in the system. All fields are mandatory. Only samples within the same collection (e.g. rock, soil, vegetation, or water) can be linked.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1379 semester 2026APRS_15
records.description: We propose a simultaneous joint observation campaign using the Parkes radio telescope and the EP satellite to observation three magnetars with known radio emission. Under simultaneous observations, we aim to investigate the correlation between their radio and X-ray emissions, including pulse profiles, flux intensity, polarization evolution, correlated multi-wavelength behavior and timing behavior.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project L126 semester 2026APRS_17
records.description: We propose a modest program to continue monitoring 4 of the 6 known radio magnetars in order to achieve three primary science goals. The first is to characterise magnetar outbursts over long timescales, for which tracking their rotational, flux density, and polarisation properties provide a clear view of the impulse response of their magnetic fields. Second, understanding the links between magnetars the mysterious fast radio burst phenomenon through the discovery of rare emission and propagation effects, shared spectro-temporal phenomenology, and connections to high-energy (X-ray/gamma-ray) phenomena. Lastly, our continued monitoring has enormous benefit to the wider magnetar community, providing rapid alerts to changes in activity, adding context to unusual behaviour detected by high-energy observations, and a host of supplementary science through the teams extensive collaborative networks. The project and its precursors have been running since 2007 and have contributed to 22 publications since then. This is the first submission since the project was converted to long-term status.

records.title: Code and data from field-experiment evaluating regional climate context dependent impacts of biocontrol agent Kordyana brasiliensis on environmental weed Tradescantia fluminensis in eastern Australia
records.description: This collection provides data collected between July 2020 and November 2025 from 97 10 m2 quadrats of invasive weed Tradescantia fluminensis abundance (volume and foliage cover), biocontrol agent Kordyana brasiliensis diseases levels (disease incidence and disease severity) and microclimate (temperature and relative humidity) and macroclimate variables (temperature and rainfall) from fourteen sites across a latitudinal gradient in NSW. This dataset was generated as part of a study to evaluate the establishment, dynamics and impacts of host specific biocontrol agent K. brasiliensis on target weed species T. fluminensis across broad spatial and temporal gradients. This collection also provides the R code (data analysis) that (1) evaluates patterns of agent establishment and disease incidence and severity across contrasting climate contexts, (2) identifies macro- and microclimatic drivers associated with variability in pathogen disease levels, and (3) assesses how variability in disease expression translates into longer term changes in T. fluminensis abundance. Please refer to the published manuscript under related links for further details (TBD)

records.title: Long-term project observations for project P1393 semester 2026APRS
records.description: An unprecedented number of non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellations have commenced operations in recent years. Satellite filings at the ITU as of October 2025 have surpassed 1.8 million active satellites to be in operation within the decade - with only about 15000 satellites in orbit today, impacting radio astronomy already significantly from both intended and unwanted emissions as well as radio radiation from the satellite platforms. This requires radio astronomy to develop, implement, and continuously verify new mitigation measures in collaboration with satellite operators. Examples of such measures which are already partially implemented for Australian radio astronomy observatories include boresight avoidance, site illumination avoidance, and frequency coordination. Ongoing measurements of out of band emissions, unwanted emissions, as well as radio radiation from satellite platform electrical and electronic systems are critical to ensure future generations of satellites are built to better electromagnetic compatibility standards. These measurements will further assist regulatory efforts by providing evidentiary basis of the impact of satellite emissions and radiation in CSIROs input to the national regulator (ACMA) as well as at the international regulatory process at the ITU. There is considerable time pressure to provide measurements within the current world radio conference (WRC27) cycle, with numerous agenda items under consideration that will have significant impact on radio astronomy if endorsed without radio astronomy input. The outcome of this work will be instrumental in improving protection of radio astronomy and help ensure there is a future for terrestrial radio astronomy in the rapidly proliferating environment of NGSO constellations.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project C3542 semester 2025OCTS
records.description: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most powerful explosions in our Universe, lending themselves as laboratories for studying the physics of relativistic outflows and shocks in astrophysical systems. In the 25+ years following the discovery of the first afterglow, only ~7 long GRBs have comprehensive enough radio monitoring to enable a rigorous inspection of the physical parameters relating to the energetics of the outflow, the density and structure of the circum-burst medium and the shock microphysics. As radio follow-up is often activated only for those with a low redshift or following optical afterglow detections, an unbiased sample of well-monitored long GRB radio afterglows is lacking. As a result, many fundamental questions remain open: (i) what is the composition of the jet and the source of the radio emission at early times?, (ii) What is the geometry of GRB outflows?, (iii) is there universality to GRB shock wave physics and do these properties evolve with time?, (iv) what are the total energy budgets of LGRBs and the nature of their environments? In particular, early- and late-time radio, on which these questions rely, are very seldom explored. Our program will answer these questions by doubling the number of long GRBs with comprehensive radio monitoring, from early (within a day) through to late (years) time, in just 3 years, establishing a complete and unbiased, multi-frequency and high cadence radio view of long GRBs. We therefore request NAPA time to trigger on and monitor 12 long GRBs per year (i.e., 6 per semester) for another 2 years.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project C1730 semester 2025OCTS
records.description: This project will observe a selection of ~200 high-energy astrophysical sources (primarily active galaxies, and a small number of gamma-ray binaries) detected by the Fermi gamma-ray satellite or ground-based TeV gamma-ray telescopes which, together with optical, X-ray and VLBI data (from the TANAMI LBA project), will enable correlations in the multi-wavelength variability of these objects to be identified and a better understanding gained of the physical processes powering these sources. Besides monitoring known sources, C1730 observations are also contributing to identifying new gamma-ray sources, both those flaring for the first time, and catalogued sources without a previously identified counterpart. An increasing focus is being placed on TeV sources and candidate high-energy neutrino sources, as part of a complementary program underway with the Effelsberg 100m telescope, and in preparation for the Cherenkov Telescope Array.

records.title: Long-term project observations for project C3363 semester 2025OCTS
records.description: The ASKAP Variables And Slow Transients (VAST; Murphy et al., 2013, 2021) commenced in November 2022. We have been allocated 2,100 hours of dedicated ASKAP time over 4 years, and in addition we have access to ~20,000 hours of commensal time for the purposes of transients analysis. The aim of the survey is to discover and study radio transient sources, from local objects such as flaring stars, through to supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. Candidate transients need to be followed up on reasonably rapid timescales, before they fade. For example supernovae and gamma-ray bursts may become undetectable before the next VAST pilot epoch (separated by approximately 2-3 months). We request NAPA time to follow up and monitor up to 20 candidate transient sources per semester, when they are detected in the VAST survey.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1419 semester 2026APRS_08
records.description: We propose a deep 100-hour Parkes radio pulsar survey of the Galactic plane region l = 240 ~ 260 deg, |b| < 2 deg, -a 80-square-degree zone currently unobserved by any major deep pulsar survey such as the Parkes Multibeam Pulsar Survey (PMPS) and The MPIfR-MeerKAT Galactic Plane Survey (MMGPS). This sightline probes the near side of the Perseus Arm (4~6 kpc), yet contains only 14 known pulsars, likely incomplete due to the shallow integrations and FFT-limited pipelines of prior work. Using the CryoPAF receiver (1100 ~ 1700 MHz, 600 MHz bandwidth) with 3000-second pointings and a Fast Folding Algorithm (FFA)-enhanced search, we will detect long-period (P=1~10s) and high-DM (< 350 pc cm ^-3) pulsars missed previously. We expect to discover 20 ~ 40 new pulsars, enabling precise mapping of the local electron density and testing Galactic ISM models. Critically, our field contains the unassociated Fermi sources , offering a prime opportunity for multiwavelength identification. The survey will also probe transient phenomena via single-pulse searches. This project addresses a well-defined observational gap with high discovery potential for both Galactic structure and high-energy astrophysics.

records.title: Small RNA sequencing of Varroa destructor from manuscript: Novel dsRNA designs increase the stability and bioefficacy of RNAi-based pesticides for Varroa destructor
records.description: Small RNA sequencing data generated from Varroa destructor mites following treatment with exogenous RNA interference (RNAi) constructs targeting the crustacean hyperglycaemic hormone (CHH) and peritrophin-A (Pero) genes. The study compares conventional double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) with structurally modified RNAi molecules, including G wobble (GU), asymmetric bulge (ASY), and loop-ended (LED) designs, to investigate how RNA structure influences siRNA biogenesis, strand bias, and RNAi efficacy. These data were produced to improve understanding of RNAi processing in V. destructor and to support the development of more effective RNAi-based control strategies for this important honey bee parasite.

records.title: iPASA.jl
records.description: iPASA is a Julia package for projected assessment of system adequacy assessment of the NEM. It couples an open Synthetic NEM network model, clustered into 15 ISP sub-regions, with AEMO 2024 Integrated System Plan (ISP) data, and evaluates adequacy metrics (LOLE, EUE, NEUE) with sequential Monte Carlo simulation via PRAS. It also enables detailed production cost modelling based on sequential unit commitment and economic dispatch simulations, supporting comprehensive assessment of operational strategies and system performance.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1413 semester 2026APRS_22
records.description: We request 75 hours of Parkes observing time for dedicated radio follow-up observations of PSR J1635-5134, a promising candidate pulsar-subdwarf B (sdB) star binary system. PSR J1635-5134 is a non-recycled 340 ms pulsar in a nearly circular 18-hour orbit with a minimum companion mass of 0.26 solar mass. It lies in a sparsely populated region of binary-pulsars parameter space and may represent a short-lived evolutionary stage immediately following inefficient spin-up, thereby providing a missing link between canonical binaries and the millisecond pulsar-WD population. The system exhibits peculiar, orbital-phase-dependent dispersion-measure (DM) variability, with DM variations exceeding 30 pc/cc, indicating substantial ionised material plausibly associated with an outflow from the companion. Moreover, during prior monitoring with Parkes, the DM variations shifted from being predominantly modest to being persistently large, implying an evolving plasma environment that cannot be characterised with sparse or irregular observations. Determining whether these high-DM variations are intermittent or long-lived, and mapping how the excess material varies with orbital phase and epoch, are essential for constraining the origin and geometry of the plasma and for testing the hypothesis that an sdB wind supplies the required electron column. Through this proposal, we aim to (i) extend the timing baseline to improve astrometric precision to sub-arcsecond accuracy, enabling secure identification of the optical counterpart in a crowded field, and (ii) perform phase-targeted observations during eclipse/DM variation phases to understand the temporal behavior of excess DM.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P595 semester 2026APRS_33
records.description: We propose to continue the PULSE@Parkes project in which high school students from Australia and around the World use the Parkes radio telescope in a remote observing model to observe and analyse pulsar data. The data from some PULSE@Parkes observations are used to support the space missions, other observations supplement the P456 Pulsar Timing Array project and the remainder were chosen in order to make a detailed analysis of pulsar timing irregularities and intermittency.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1394 semester 2026APRS_02
records.description: We propose to observe the radio-loud magnetar 1E 1547.0-5408 to support an upcoming campaign with NASA's Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) to confirm the first ever direct detection of vacuum birefringence. This strong-field quantum effect was first predicted by Heisenberg back in the 1930s, but has eluded direct detection in Earth-based laboratories due to our inability to replicate the magnetic field strengths required to induce vacuum birefreingence. 1E 1547.0-5408 displays a high X-ray polarisation fraction with a strong energy and rotation-phase dependence, along with evidence of mode-locking in the polarisation position angle. Both effects are strong indicators that vacuum birefringence is occurring in the magnetised atmosphere of this extreme object. Our observations with Murriyang will not only provide a phase-coherent timing solution for folding the IXPE photons during the upcoming 2026 campaign, but provides a critical, independent measure of the magnetar viewing and magnetic geometry. Combined, these measurements will confirm this long sought direct of vacuum birefrinegnce, thereby opening a new window into studying quantum electrodynamics in one of the most extreme environments in the Universe.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1398 semester 2026APRS_16
records.description: Low-frequency (< ~1 GHz) Galactic-plane pulsar surveys are strongly limited by sky background noise, interstellar scattering, and dispersion smearing, leading to an incomplete census of the pulsar population. High-frequency (> 2 GHz) observations mitigate these effects and have recently enabled the discovery of pulsars that remain undetectable at low-frequency. We analyzed archival data from the 2008 Parkes 6.5-GHz pulsar survey using modern search techniques. This reprocessing has revealed four previously unknown millisecond pulsar candidates with spin periods of 3-11 ms and dispersion measures of 20-170 pc/cc. Two candidates exhibit significant line-of-sight acceleration, indicating likely membership in compact binary systems. We request a total of 8.4 hours of follow-up observations with the Parkes (Murriyang) Ultra-Wideband Low (UWL) receiver to confirm these candidates and characterize their emission across 704-4032 MHz. Confirming these sources would expand the population of high-frequency selected pulsars and demonstrate the continued importance of high-frequency searches for uncovering exotic systems obscured in conventional low-frequency surveys.

records.title: Parkes observations for project P1402 semester 2026APRS_24
records.description: We propose a dedicated Parkes/Murriyang timing campaign of the newly confirmed narrow-duty cycle (~6 %) millisecond pulsar (MSP) PSR J2147-3604. This source was identified in a reprocessing of the Green Bank North Celestial Cap (GBNCC) survey as a high-confidence candidate with a spin period of 3.2 ms, and a dispersion measure, DM of 17 pc/cc. The pulsar was subsequently confirmed by the Fermi--TRAPUM collaboration via MeerKAT beamforming localisation and Parkes follow-up. Parkes/UWL observations allocated using green time detected this pulsar between 700--1500~MHz, and confirmed that it's in a binary system. Due to its low DM, we also detected strong interstellar scintillation. We request 35~hr of Murriyang time using the UWL receiver and APOLLO backend to obtain a phase-coherent timing solution and to characterise its spin, orbital, and propagation properties. Since the pulsar is also associated with a FERMI source, a precise radio ephemeris will also enable sensitive searches for gamma-ray pulsations in Fermi-LAT data and assess PSR J2147-3604's suitability for pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) and future gamma-ray timing applications.
